content.title: About
content.content: Taro leaves, cooked are the edible leaves of the taro plant (Colocasia esculenta) that have been boiled. The leaves have a mild, slightly nutty flavor and a soft texture. They are used in traditional Southeast Asian dishes, soups, stews, and as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Taro is an ancient cultivated crop, known for more than 9,000 years.
The leaves are high in starch, so boiling removes bitterness and makes them palatable.
In some cultures taro leaves are considered a symbol of prosperity and are used in rituals.
Taro is grown in tropical and subtropical regions, but leaf production can be extended to temperate zones with frost protection.
Traditionally in Hawaii, taro leaves are baked in the ground to make a dish called "luau".

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps maintain gut health.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C is an antioxidant that supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports normal heart function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Taro leaves contain virtually no fat, making them suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Provides vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 is involved in protein metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: High oxalate levels may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Toxic if undercooked
items.content: Raw or undercooked taro leaves contain calcium oxalate crystals that can irritate the stomach.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some people may be allergic to taro plant proteins.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked taro leaves can be added to soups, curries, vegetable stews, or served as a side dish with rice and meat. They are often sliced into strips and lightly sautéed after boiling for a gentle crisp.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked taro leaves in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze them in portion‑sized bags.
